pages.title: The Studio
pages.content:
The Garden Studio

A Boutique Garden Studio in West London

Welcome to Anat Handmade Pottery, a sanctuary tucked away in the heart of Ealing. This light-filled garden studio was designed specifically for beginners and improvers who seek more than just a class—it is a place for hands-on guidance and artistic growth.


The studio is fully equipped with professional wheels, hand-building tools, and a kiln, all thoughtfully arranged to maintain a calm and inspiring atmosphere. Surrounded by natural light and garden greenery, it offers the perfect setting to slow down, relax, and reconnect with your creativity.


Here, we leave the rush of the city behind. It is a quiet escape where you can breathe, enjoy the tactile nature of clay, and experience the simple joy of creating something beautiful with your own hands.

The Details

Located in South Ealing, West London. A short walk from South Ealing Station (Piccadilly Line) and accessible via bus routes 65 and E3. Details and directions provided upon booking.

pages.title: About Me
pages.content:
The Journey from MBA to Mud

Artist, Teacher, and Founder of Anat Handmade Pottery

My love for ceramics started when I was just eight years old. It was a childhood passion that stayed with me, even as I moved into the business world to complete my BSc and MBA. But no matter how far I went in my career, I always found myself drawn back to the potter's wheel. Eventually, I decided to leave the corporate path behind to follow my heart and become a full-time potter.

I studied at the Bezalel Academy of Arts and Design, where I truly learned the craft and technical side of working with clay. During those years of study, I opened my first studio, discovering how much I loved both creating my own pieces and teaching others how to do the same.

Now, I work from my boutique garden studio in West London, creating porcelain and stoneware pieces. My work is all about the details. I love combining the clean lines of wheel-throwing with colourful slips and screen prints that I produce myself.

For me, pottery is a way to slow down and be present. Whether I’m working on a new collection or helping a student during a workshop, my goal is to share the simple, handmade joy that comes from working with clay.

Anat Varon Moneta

Good to Know

I’ve never touched clay before; is that okay?

Absolutely. All workshops are designed for beginners, focusing on the joy of the process. A small tip: working with clay is easier with shorter nails, and I recommend leaving rings or bracelets at home.

What should I wear to class?

Comfortable clothes and shoes you don’t mind getting dusty. Clay washes out easily, but aprons are provided for all sessions.

Where is the studio located?

My garden studio is in South Ealing, London W5. A short walk from South Ealing Station and Northfields Station (Piccadilly Line) and well-served by the 65, E2 and E3 buses. The full address and arrival instructions will be sent once your booking is confirmed.

Can I book a class as a gift?

Yes! Please mention this in your message and I can provide a digital or physical gift voucher for the recipient.

When can I collect my pots?

Pottery is a slow craft; pieces need to dry thoroughly before their two firings. Your work will typically be ready in 3–4 weeks. Because my studio has limited storage space, I can only hold finished pieces for 2 months. After this time, uncollected work may be re-homed or recycled.

What is your booking and cancellation policy?

If you can’t make it to your session, just let me know as soon as possible. We can easily reschedule you to a different date or arrange a make-up session so you don’t miss out on the clay. If you’d prefer a refund, I’m happy to provide one up to 48 hours before the class.

Do you ship pottery?

If you are visiting from outside London and cannot collect your pieces, I am happy to arrange shipping for an additional fee to cover safe packaging and postage.

posts.title: Student Spotlight: A 4-Week Wheel Throwing Journey
posts.content:
I often get asked, "Can I really make something I’d actually use in just four weeks?" The answer is a resounding yes.

Today, I'm sharing the journey of one of my recent students, Natalie, who joined my Throwing Journey for Adults. Over the course of four sessions, she went from learning how to center a ball of clay to taking home a set of custom-illustrated bowls. Here is a look at her process from start to finish.

Week 1 & 2: Finding the Form

The journey always begins on the wheel. The first few sessions are all about "centering" - getting the clay to cooperate with your hands.

In this photo from the start of the course, you can see the focus required to pull the walls of the bowl up. It’s a delicate balance of strength and gentleness.

Once the clay has dried to a "leather hard" state (usually by the next session), we move to trimming. This is where we carve away the excess clay to reveal the elegant shape underneath and create a foot ring. It’s often the most satisfying part of the process - watching the ribbons of clay fly off!

Week 3: Adding Personality

Once the form is finalized, the wheel stops, and the creativity really begins. Natalie chose to hand-paint a delicate tiger design using underglazes. This stage is where a simple clay bowl becomes your bowl.

Week 4 - The Final Transformation (Glazing)

The final session of the Throwing Journey is dedicated to glazing. After the pieces have been through their first "bisque" firing, the student returns to apply the glazes. This is where the student applies what will turn out to be the shiny glassy coat of their work. Usually, they will apply a clear glaze to allow the natural beauty of the clay and their earlier decorations to shine through.

Once glazed, the pieces head back into the kiln for one last high-temperature firing. After the transformation will be complete, these unique, handmade pieces will be ready for their new home.

The Final Result

After the final glaze firing, the colours pop, the clay turns to stone, and the piece is ready for the kitchen. Here are the finished pieces: a beautiful set of bowls with a whimsical tiger pattern. They are food-safe, dishwasher-safe, and completely unique.

Start Your Own Journey

You don’t need to consider yourself an "artist" to create something beautiful. You just need to show up and get your hands dirty. Book your spot in the Throwing Journey for Adults :

posts.title: The Journey of a Mug: From Raw Clay to Your Morning Coffee
posts.content:
Working with clay is a lesson in patience and transformation. Each mug that leaves my garden studio in Ealing is part of a larger Throwing Journey. It begins as a humble lump of clay and undergoes a multi-stage journey before it ever reaches your hands.

Because the process involves drying stages and two separate kiln firings, a finished mug takes a few weeks to complete.

Here is a behind-the-scenes look at how a mug comes to life at my studio.

1. Preparing the Foundation

Every piece starts with wedging. This is the process of kneading the clay to remove air bubbles and ensure an even consistency. Without proper wedging, a pot can crack in the kiln.

2. At the Potter’s Wheel

Once the clay is prepared, it’s time to find a rhythm at the wheel. I center the clay and pull the walls upward to create the thrown pot. At this stage, the clay is still soft and "wet", full of potential but very delicate.

3. Refining the Form: Trimming

After the pot has dried to a "leather-hard" state, I return it to the wheel for trimming. This is where I carve away excess clay from the bottom and create a foot ring, giving the mug a refined shape and a lighter feel.

4. The Art of the Handle

Handles are pulled by hand to ensure they are esthetic, uniform and comfortable to hold. Once shaped, they must rest and dry slightly until they match the moisture level of the mug body.

5. Bringing it Together

Attaching the handle is a precise task. I "score and slip" both surfaces: scratching the clay and adding liquid clay "glue" to create a permanent bond that will survive drying process and the intense heat of the kiln.

6. Adding Character: Surface Decoration

Now for the creative details. Using brushes and sponges, I apply surface decoration. This is where the mug begins to take on its unique personality through color and texture.

7. The Final Transformation: Fire and Shrinkage

The most surprising part of the journey is the final result. Pottery undergoes a massive physical change during firing. You can clearly see the shrinkage when comparing a raw clay mug to a finished, fired piece. The heat draws out every last drop of moisture and vitrifies the clay into a durable, functional piece of art.

Master the Entire Process

Because a single session isn't enough to see a mug through from raw clay to a finished, glazed piece, I invite you to join me for a complete Throwing Journey. The reason why I call my 4-week course a 'Throwing Journey' is because you are traveling through every stage of the clay's life, from the wheel to the final firing.

In this 4-week 1:1 private course, you will move through every stage featured in this post: from the first wedge of clay to the final glazing process.

  • Duration: 4 Sessions (2.5 Hours each)
  • Cost: £320 (Private 1:1 tuition)
  • Location: South Ealing garden studio
